AI Cybersecurity  ·  OT Security You cannot turn it off to fix it.

In operational technology (OT), the plants, control systems and field equipment that keep physical processes running, the attacker’s objective is rarely data. It is visibility, control and the ability to keep running safely. So every recommendation is written against a maintenance window.

6–12 WEEKSWRITTEN AGAINST YOUR MAINTENANCE WINDOWSSAFETY CASE RESPECTED
The decisions underneath

Three questions decide the design.

OT security fails when a corporate playbook is applied to an estate that cannot accept it. These are the three questions that keep it honest.

01

Do the two estates really fail independently

Shared identity, shared DNS, and an engineering laptop that lives on both sides. Independence is asserted far more often than it is verified.

02

Who owns the crossing

The single most common blank on an org chart is the boundary between corporate IT and operations. Both sides assume the other holds it.

03

What can you actually change, and when

A change that needs an unscheduled outage won’t get made. Sequencing changes against real maintenance windows is most of the work.

The boundary

We map and sequence. The safety-case holder decides.

This is an assessment. We map the crossing and write the plan. The people who hold the safety case decide what changes and when.

STEP 01 · ORVIX

We map the crossing

We find every asset, protocol and connection between the corporate and operational networks, passively where active scanning would be unsafe. Then we test whether the two really fail independently.

STEP 02 · SAFETY-CASE HOLDER

Your operations team makes the change

Changes on a running plant belong to whoever holds the safety case, inside a window they control. We give them a sequenced, window-ready change plan.

STEP 03 · ORVIX

We verify after each window

After each maintenance window we check that the change held and update the crossing map, so the plan stays current.

Every recommendation is written for a real maintenance window. That is what makes it usable on a plant that cannot stop.

Questions we are asked

Before you ask us.

Will you scan our production network?
Only with explicit written agreement that active scanning is safe on the specific segment and equipment. The default is passive discovery, because a slower assessment is always better than an outage caused by one.
Our OT network is air-gapped (physically separate). Do we need this?
Testing that claim is usually the first useful output of the engagement. Engineering laptops, remote vendor support, historian replication and shared identity often connect the two sides, and we document each link we find.
Who patches our controllers?
Patching belongs to whoever holds the safety case, inside a window they control. We give them a sequenced, window-ready change plan: what needs to change and the order to do it in.
How does this relate to the detection service?
A crossing map makes detection placement possible on the operational side. Where we also run Managed Detection & Response, its effectiveness is tested by a party outside the team operating it.

Start with the crossing that has no owner.

If you cannot immediately name who owns the boundary between your corporate and operational networks, that is the conversation. It takes thirty minutes.
